rv: An election goes to the dogs

A Scottish blowhard's candidacy appears to be in the bag, but then all hell breaks loose over an unpaid dog license. (You can be forgiven for thinking of Frank Capra.) The complete print is in very good condition. However it is low in contrast,

Except for the references to current events, this really feels much more contemporary. It feels more like late forties to early 1960's movie--maybe even a little like MASH (t.v.). This was a little bit sharper than a typical screwball comedy, but never cynical. Very British, very timely in terms of it's message, but timeless as well.

Thoroughly mad cap British humour. The local Provost has his pride cause him to take one poorly advised action after another against a woman and her dog. Along the way his daughter finds a reporter to be just the man for her. You will enjoy this film.
This film was released on November 1937, not February 1937!

I checked a 1977 biography of Vivien Leigh, and this film was released on November 1937 (US), not February 1937, as AFI Catalog claimed. According to Copyright Catalog and AFI Catalog, this film's copyright date was August 10, 1937. The film stock and the story description were deposited in October 1937, less than three months after first US publication.

rv: An excellent look at real radio from the late 40s

Decades ago when I was program director of a local station, I owned a 16 mm print of this years ago and would show it to community civic groups. They enjoyed the nostalgia aspect and my description of how radio had adapted to change in the 1950's. It is an excellent look at the business before TV took over as the dominant home entertainment media.

It is refreshing to see a piece about the radio scene as it was rather than how folks wished it to be. The quote that placed the ratio of good shows with dreck at 20 to 1 is pretty spot on. So much is now lost to us but even what remains bears out that the gems were indeed well buried in the dross. Seeing Fibber McGee and Molly in action was well worth the price of admission, the honest look at the industry and the better intentions of some of it's workers was a much welcome find.
